references.text: The requirement for a male without defect from the herd for the burnt offering is repeated here, emphasizing that the sacrifice must be unblemished to be accepted by the Lord.
The sacrificial animal must be without defect (תָּמִים) to be accepted, paralleling the requirement in 1:3.
At the consecration of the priests, a young bull and two rams without defect are required, demonstrating the consistent demand for unblemished sacrifices.
The altar of burnt offering is placed before the entrance to the tabernacle (אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד), which is the place where the sacrifice is to be presented.
All offerings must be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting before the Lord, corresponding with the location specified in 1:3.
Ezekiel prophesies about future sacrifices of unblemished animals, linking back to the original requirement in Leviticus.
Christ offered himself without defect (ἄμωμον) to God, fulfilling the Old Testament requirement for an unblemished sacrifice.
Christ is compared to a lamb without blemish or spot (ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου), fulfilling the sacrificial requirement of an animal without defect.
Christ gave himself as an offering and a fragrant aroma to God, fulfilling the burnt offering that was brought before the Lord.
Extends the rules for burnt offerings from cattle to sheep with identical requirements for consecration.
Describes identical ritual actions (presentation at the entrance) for different types of sacrifices.
Highlights that the principle of wholeness as a burnt offering applies regardless of the type of animal.
